lesson.title: One Base, Many Consequences: What Point Mutations Really Change
lesson.summary: A point mutation swaps a single nucleotide base for another in a DNA sequence, and depending on exactly where it lands and what it changes it to, that one letter change can be harmless, damaging, or anything in between.
lesson.body:
Every time a cell divides, its DNA polymerase must copy billions of base pairs with extraordinary accuracy, correctly matching each A with a T and each G with a C as described by the base pairing rules. Even with proofreading, mistakes occasionally slip through, and a single base in the new strand ends up paired incorrectly or is later altered by a chemical change to the DNA. When that single incorrect base survives to become a permanent part of the genome, it is called a point mutation: the substitution of one nucleotide base for another at one position in the sequence.

Because the genetic code is read in three letter codons, a single substituted base changes at most one codon, and the effect of that change depends entirely on what amino acid, if any, the new codon specifies. Consider the codon UCA, which normally codes for the amino acid serine. Changing its third base from A to G gives UCG, which still codes for serine: no change to the protein at all. Changing its first base from U to C instead gives CCA, which codes for proline, a different amino acid at that position in the protein. And changing its second base from C to A gives UAA, one of the three stop codons, which halts protein synthesis at that point rather than adding an amino acid at all. Three different single base changes to the very same starting codon, three very different outcomes. These three categories, no change in amino acid, a changed amino acid, and a premature stop, are called silent, missense, and nonsense mutations, and each gets its own closer look in the chapters that follow.

Not every point mutation even reaches a codon. A substitution in DNA that lies between genes, in an intron, or in a region that does not end up in the final protein sequence may have no effect on any protein at all. A substitution inside a regulatory sequence, such as a promoter or an operator, can change how much of a gene's product is made without changing the product's sequence at all, an idea that becomes important once regulation of gene expression enters the picture later in this unit. Geneticists also distinguish transitions, where a purine is swapped for the other purine, A to G or G to A, or a pyrimidine for the other pyrimidine, C to T or T to C, from transversions, where a purine is swapped for a pyrimidine or vice versa. Transitions tend to happen more often than transversions, largely because swapping between two chemically similar ring structures is an easier mistake for replication and repair machinery to make than swapping between structurally different ones.

What a point mutation does not do is disturb anything beyond the single codon it touches. Every codon on either side of the change is read exactly as it was before. That property is what sets point mutations apart from the other major class of small scale mutation, the frameshift, where adding or removing bases throws off the reading frame for everything downstream. That comparison is the subject of the next chapter.
